name: Learn: Autoscaling (HPA)
objective: CKAD › Application Deployment. Create HorizontalPodAutoscalers: imperative autoscale, autoscaling/v2 with memory and multiple metrics, scaling behavior, and the no-requests diagnose-fix. Graded on the HPA object (this bench has no metrics-server, so actual scaling needs one).
description: Five strict HPA practicals against pre-seeded Deployments. Each Check shows which requirements you met and why any failed.

questions.title: Autoscale a Deployment (imperative)
questions.teach:
An **HPA** scales a Deployment's replicas on observed metrics. Create one fast: `kubectl autoscale deployment <d> --name <h> --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10`.

**Gotcha:** the target Deployment must set resource **requests** for that metric, or the HPA can't compute utilization (shows `<unknown>`).
questions.prompt:
In `hpa-learn`, create an HPA named `web-hpa` for Deployment `web`: target **70%** average CPU, min **2**, max **10**.

Target: `web-hpa` → scaleTargetRef `web`, minReplicas 2, maxReplicas 10, CPU Utilization 70%.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n hpa-learn autoscale deployment web --name web-hpa --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa web-hpa
questions.eli5:
Think of an **HPA (HorizontalPodAutoscaler)** as a **thermostat for your app**. You don't adjust the heat by hand — you set a target ("keep it around 70°") and the thermostat adds or removes heat to hold that number. An HPA does the same, but instead of temperature it watches **CPU usage**, and instead of heat it adds or removes **Pod copies (replicas)**.

The fastest way to install this thermostat is one command:

```bash
kubectl autoscale deployment web --name web-hpa --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10
```

That says: "Watch Deployment `web`. Try to keep average CPU at **70%**. Never go below **2** copies, never above **10**." When the app gets busy and CPU climbs past 70%, the HPA adds Pods; when it's quiet, it removes them (down to the floor of 2).

The sneaky part: **"70% of what?"** CPU percentage is measured against the amount of CPU you **requested** for the container. If you never told Kubernetes "this container needs 100m of CPU," the thermostat has no baseline — it can't turn a raw usage number into a percentage, and it just shows `<unknown>`.

**Watch out for:**

- **The Deployment MUST set CPU `requests`.** No request → the HPA shows `<unknown>` and can't scale. (This is the exact bug you fix in a later step.)
- **A metrics-server must be running** to feed CPU readings. This bench has none, so real scaling won't happen — you're graded on the HPA object itself.
- **`min` and `max` are hard limits.** The HPA will not scale below min or above max no matter how busy things get.
- **`kubectl autoscale` only does CPU.** For memory or custom metrics you must write YAML (next steps).
questions.deepDive:
## Autoscale a Deployment (imperative) — full rundown

### Mental model
A **HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)** is a controller that periodically compares an **observed metric** against a **target** and adjusts the replica count of a scale target (Deployment/ReplicaSet/StatefulSet) to close the gap. It scales **out/in** (more/fewer Pods) — never bigger Pods (that's the VPA).

Core formula:
```
desiredReplicas = ceil( currentReplicas × ( currentMetric / targetMetric ) )
```
clamped to `[minReplicas, maxReplicas]`.

### The imperative command
```bash
kubectl autoscale deployment web \
  --name web-hpa \
  --cpu-percent=70 \
  --min=2 \
  --max=10
```
| Flag | Maps to | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `deployment web` | `scaleTargetRef` kind+name | the thing being scaled |
| `--name web-hpa` | `metadata.name` | HPA object name (defaults to target name if omitted) |
| `--cpu-percent=70` | CPU Resource metric, 70% avg util | CPU only via this command |
| `--min=2` | `spec.minReplicas` | floor |
| `--max=10` | `spec.maxReplicas` | ceiling (required) |

### Equivalent YAML (autoscaling/v2)
```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web-hpa
  namespace: hpa-learn
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
```

### How CPU % is computed
`averageUtilization` is a **percentage of the sum of container CPU `requests`** across the Pod, averaged over all Pods:
```
utilization% = (avg actual CPU across pods) / (CPU request) × 100
```
No request → **no denominator** → metric is `<unknown>` and the HPA cannot act.

### Inspecting
```bash
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa web-hpa
# NAME      REFERENCE        TARGETS         MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS
# web-hpa   Deployment/web   12%/70%         2         10        2
kubectl -n hpa-learn describe hpa web-hpa      # events + why it scaled
```

### API versions
| Version | Status | Capability |
|---|---|---|
| `autoscaling/v1` | legacy | CPU utilization only |
| `autoscaling/v2` | **current** | CPU, memory, custom, external, multiple metrics, behavior |

`kubectl autoscale` creates whatever the cluster default serializes to (often v1-shaped for CPU), but you read/write v2 for anything richer.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Target needs resource `requests`.** Utilization is a % of the request; missing request → `<unknown>/70%`.
- **`metrics-server` must be installed** for Resource metrics to populate. On a bench without it, TARGETS stays `<unknown>` and no scaling occurs — you're graded on the HPA definition.
- **`--max` is mandatory**; `--min` defaults to 1 if omitted.
- **One HPA per workload.** Pointing two HPAs (or an HPA + manual `kubectl scale`) at the same Deployment causes fighting.
- **Don't set `replicas` on a Deployment that an HPA manages** — the HPA owns the replica count; a fixed `replicas` in your manifest fights the HPA on every apply.
- HPA will not scale a Deployment to **0** (min is ≥1 for the classic HPA).

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n hpa-learn autoscale deployment web \
  --name web-hpa --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa web-hpa
```

questions.title: HPA v2 on memory
questions.teach:
The `autoscaling/v2` HPA scales on any metric via `spec.metrics`. A **Resource** metric on memory: `{type: Resource, resource: {name: memory, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 80}}}`.

**Gotcha:** `kubectl autoscale` only does CPU — for memory/custom metrics you write the v2 YAML.
questions.prompt:
In `hpa-learn`, create HPA `api-hpa` (`autoscaling/v2`) for Deployment `api`: scale on **memory** at **80%** average utilization, min **1**, max **6**.

Target: `api-hpa` → api, a Resource/memory metric at 80% Utilization, min 1, max 6.
questions.hint: Write the v2 YAML with `metrics: [{type: Resource, resource: {name: memory, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 80}}}]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: api-hpa, namespace: hpa-learn }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api }
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 6
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: memory, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 80 } }
YAML

verification.description: api-hpa -> api, memory Utilization 80%, min 1, max 6

questions.eli5:
In the last step your thermostat watched **CPU**. But sometimes CPU isn't the thing that's maxing out — your app might be fine on CPU while slowly filling up its **memory**, like a kitchen counter piling up with dishes. You want the thermostat to watch the **dishes (memory)** instead and add more helpers when it gets too full.

Here's the catch: the quick one-liner `kubectl autoscale` is a **CPU-only gadget**. It literally has no knob for memory. So to watch memory, you have to **write the full recipe yourself** in YAML, using the modern `autoscaling/v2` format.

The important piece is the `metrics` list, where you describe exactly what to watch:

```yaml
metrics:
- type: Resource
  resource:
    name: memory
    target:
      type: Utilization
      averageUtilization: 80
```

Read that like a sentence: "It's a **Resource** metric, specifically **memory**, and I want the average to stay around **80%**." Plus `minReplicas: 1` and `maxReplicas: 6` as the floor and ceiling.

Just like CPU, "80%" means **80% of the memory you *requested*** for the container — so the Deployment still needs a memory `request` set, or you'll see `<unknown>`.

**Watch out for:**

- **`kubectl autoscale` can't do memory** — you must write v2 YAML. This is the whole point of the step.
- **Must use `apiVersion: autoscaling/v2`** (not v1). v1 only understands CPU.
- **The Deployment needs a memory `requests`** value, or utilization can't be computed.
- **`target.type` is `Utilization`** (a percentage). There's also `AverageValue` (an absolute amount like `200Mi`) — don't mix them up; Utilization needs a request, AverageValue doesn't.
- **Spelling matters**: the resource name is lowercase `memory`, and the field is `averageUtilization`.
questions.deepDive:
## HPA v2 on memory — full rundown

### Mental model
The `autoscaling/v2` HPA scales on **any** metric listed under `spec.metrics`. Each entry has a `type` (Resource / Pods / Object / External / ContainerResource) and a `target`. For memory you use a **Resource** metric named `memory` with a **Utilization** target. The imperative `kubectl autoscale` shortcut is CPU-only, so memory **requires** hand-written v2 YAML.

### Metric types (v2)
| `type` | What it measures | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `Resource` | CPU/memory of pods vs their **request** | cpu / memory utilization |
| `ContainerResource` | same, but a **named container** | memory of just the `app` container |
| `Pods` | a custom per-pod metric, averaged | queue depth per pod |
| `Object` | a metric describing one object | Ingress requests/sec |
| `External` | a metric outside the cluster | cloud queue length |

### Target types
| `target.type` | Field | Meaning | Needs a request? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Utilization` | `averageUtilization` (int %) | % of the resource **request** | ✅ yes |
| `AverageValue` | `averageValue` (quantity) | absolute avg per pod (e.g. `200Mi`) | ❌ no |
| `Value` | `value` (quantity) | a single total value (Object/External) | ❌ no |

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api-hpa
  namespace: hpa-learn
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 6
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80
```

### Why not `kubectl autoscale`?
```bash
kubectl autoscale deployment api --cpu-percent=80 ...   # ONLY cpu
# there is no --memory-percent flag
```
Fast path to the YAML scaffold:
```bash
kubectl autoscale deployment api --cpu-percent=80 --min=1 --max=6 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > api-hpa.yaml
# then edit: change cpu -> memory, ensure apiVersion is autoscaling/v2
```
(Simplest on the exam is to just write the v2 YAML directly.)

### How memory utilization is computed
```
utilization% = (avg working-set memory across pods) / (memory request) × 100
```
Target `averageUtilization: 80` → HPA tries to keep that at 80%. No memory `request` on the container → `<unknown>`.

### Inspecting
```bash
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa api-hpa
# TARGETS shows e.g. 45%/80%  (memory)
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa api-hpa -o yaml | grep -A6 metrics
kubectl -n hpa-learn describe hpa api-hpa
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Memory needs v2 YAML** — the imperative command cannot do it.
- **Must set `apiVersion: autoscaling/v2`.** Under v1 the memory metric silently disappears when the server down-converts.
- **Deployment needs a memory `requests`** for `Utilization` to work.
- **`Utilization` vs `AverageValue`**: Utilization = % of request (needs request); AverageValue = absolute `Mi`/`Gi` per pod (no request needed). Picking the wrong one is a classic error.
- **Memory doesn't scale *down* gracefully** in reality — processes rarely release memory, so memory-based scale-in can be sticky. (Conceptual, not graded here.)
- Resource name is lowercase `memory`; the field is `averageUtilization` (camelCase).

### Quick reference
```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: api-hpa, namespace: hpa-learn }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api }
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 6
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: memory, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 80 } }
```

questions.title: HPA with multiple metrics
questions.teach:
A v2 HPA can list **several** metrics — it scales to satisfy the one demanding the most replicas. Combine CPU and memory under `spec.metrics`.

**Gotcha:** the HPA takes the **max** desired replicas across all metrics, not the average.
questions.prompt:
In `hpa-learn`, create HPA `cache-hpa` for Deployment `cache` with **two** metrics — CPU at **60%** and memory at **75%** average utilization — min **2**, max **8**.

Target: `cache-hpa` → cache, both CPU(60%) and memory(75%) Resource metrics, min 2, max 8.
questions.hint: Two entries under `metrics:` — one `resource: {name: cpu, ...averageUtilization: 60}` and one `name: memory, ...75`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: cache-hpa, namespace: hpa-learn }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: cache }
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 8
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } }
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: memory, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 75 } }
YAML

verification.description: cache-hpa -> cache, cpu 60% + memory 75%, min 2, max 8

questions.eli5:
Now give your thermostat **two sensors at once** — one watching CPU, one watching memory. Like a smart home that adds air conditioning if *either* the room gets hot **or** the humidity gets high. You don't want it to average the two and get a lukewarm answer; you want it to react to whichever one is screaming loudest.

That's exactly how a multi-metric HPA behaves. You list both metrics, and the HPA calculates "how many Pods would I need to satisfy CPU?" and "how many for memory?" — then **picks the bigger number**. Whichever metric demands the most replicas wins. This keeps you safe: it never under-provisions by averaging a calm metric with a panicking one.

```yaml
metrics:
- type: Resource
  resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } }
- type: Resource
  resource: { name: memory, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 75 } }
```

So: CPU target 60%, memory target 75%, with a floor of 2 Pods and a ceiling of 8.

**Watch out for:**

- **It takes the MAX, not the average.** If CPU says "need 4 Pods" and memory says "need 6," you get **6**. This is the single most-tested fact here.
- **Every metric needs its matching `request`.** CPU target needs a CPU request; memory target needs a memory request. If one metric reads `<unknown>`, the HPA leans on the others but you've lost that safety net.
- **Both entries are items in the same `metrics:` list** — two `- type: Resource` bullets, not one entry with two resources.
- **Still `autoscaling/v2`** — multiple metrics don't exist in v1.
- Scale-*down* only happens when **all** metrics agree it's safe; one busy metric keeps replicas high.
questions.deepDive:
## HPA with multiple metrics — full rundown

### Mental model
A v2 HPA may list **several metrics** under `spec.metrics`. For each metric the controller independently computes a desired replica count, then takes the **maximum** across all of them. The idea: scale to satisfy the **most demanding** signal so no dimension is starved.

```
desired = max( desiredFromCPU, desiredFromMemory, ... )  clamped to [min, max]
```

### Why max, not average
If you averaged, a calm metric would mask a hot one and you'd under-provision. Taking the max guarantees every metric's target is met or beaten. Scale-**in** only happens when **every** metric's computed desired count is lower (and the scaleDown stabilization window allows it).

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: cache-hpa
  namespace: hpa-learn
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: cache
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 8
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 60
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 75
```

### Worked example
Current = 3 replicas.
| Metric | Current | Target | desired = ceil(3 × cur/target) |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | 90% | 60% | ceil(3 × 1.5) = 5 |
| Memory | 50% | 75% | ceil(3 × 0.67) = 2 |

HPA picks **max(5, 2) = 5** replicas (within 2–8).

### Requirements per metric
Each Resource/Utilization metric needs the matching **request** on the container:
- CPU metric → container CPU `requests`
- Memory metric → container memory `requests`

A metric with no request resolves to `<unknown>` and is effectively ignored (the others still drive scaling), losing that dimension's protection.

### Inspecting
```bash
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa cache-hpa
# TARGETS: cpu: 45%/60%, memory: 60%/75%
kubectl -n hpa-learn describe hpa cache-hpa     # shows per-metric current/target + which one drove the decision
```

### Mixing metric types
You can combine Resource + Pods/Object/External in the same list — the max rule still applies. CKAD focus is CPU+memory Resource metrics, but the mechanism is identical for custom metrics.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **MAX across metrics, never average** — the headline fact.
- **Two list items**, each `- type: Resource` with its own `resource` block. Do not try to cram cpu and memory into one entry.
- **Each metric needs its own request** or it reads `<unknown>`.
- **`autoscaling/v2` required** — v1 cannot express multiple metrics.
- Scale-down is conservative: it waits for **all** metrics to be below target **and** respects the scaleDown stabilization window (next step).
- Indentation: `target` is nested under `resource`, which is nested under the list item.

### Quick reference
```yaml
metrics:
- type: Resource
  resource: { name: cpu,    target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } }
- type: Resource
  resource: { name: memory, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 75 } }
# HPA uses max(desired_cpu, desired_mem), clamped to [minReplicas, maxReplicas]
```

questions.title: Tune scaling behavior
questions.teach:
`spec.behavior` controls how fast the HPA scales. A `scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` makes it wait before scaling in, to avoid flapping.

**Gotcha:** behavior is split into `scaleUp` and `scaleDown`; the stabilization window smooths the decision over that lookback.
questions.prompt:
In `hpa-learn`, create HPA `worker-hpa` for Deployment `worker`: CPU **50%**, min **1**, max **5**, and a **scaleDown** `stabilizationWindowSeconds` of **300**.

Target: `worker-hpa` → worker, CPU 50%, min 1, max 5, behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds 300.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: worker-hpa, namespace: hpa-learn }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: worker }
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 5
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 50 } }
  behavior:
    scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 }
YAML

verification.description: worker-hpa: CPU 50%, min 1, max 5, scaleDown stabilization 300

questions.eli5:
Imagine your thermostat is a bit **twitchy**: the moment the room cools for one minute, it shuts off the heat — then it's cold again, so it blasts back on. On, off, on, off. That constant flip-flopping is called **flapping**, and it's bad for both heaters and Pods (starting and killing Pods repeatedly is wasteful and disruptive).

The fix is to tell the thermostat: **"before you turn things DOWN, wait a while and make sure it's really calm."** In HPA land that's the **`behavior`** block, specifically a **scale-down stabilization window**.

```yaml
behavior:
  scaleDown:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
```

`stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300` means: "When deciding whether to remove Pods, look back over the last **300 seconds (5 minutes)** and use the **highest** replica recommendation from that window." So a brief dip in load won't immediately shrink your app — it has to stay quiet for a full 5 minutes before Pods are removed. Scaling **up** stays snappy (you want to react fast to load); only scaling **down** is deliberately patient.

**Watch out for:**

- **`behavior` has two halves: `scaleUp` and `scaleDown`.** They're configured separately. Here you only set `scaleDown`.
- **The window smooths the *decision*, not a timer.** During the window the HPA uses the **max** recommended replicas, so it won't drop below a recent peak until things truly settle.
- **Default scale-down window is already 300s**; scale-up default is 0s (immediate). You're making the intent explicit.
- **`behavior` is `autoscaling/v2` only** — it doesn't exist in v1.
- Don't confuse `stabilizationWindowSeconds` with `policies` (rate limits like "at most 10% down per minute) — they're siblings under `scaleDown`.
questions.deepDive:
## Tune scaling behavior — full rundown

### Mental model
`spec.behavior` lets you control **how aggressively** an HPA changes replica count, independently for **scaling up** and **scaling down**. Each direction has:
- a **stabilization window** (look-back smoothing), and
- a set of **policies** (rate limits) plus a `selectPolicy`.

The classic knob is `scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds`, which dampens flapping by reusing the recent **max** recommendation before shrinking.

### The structure
```yaml
behavior:
  scaleUp:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0        # default 0 (react immediately)
    selectPolicy: Max                    # Max | Min | Disabled
    policies:
    - { type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 15 }
    - { type: Pods,    value: 4,   periodSeconds: 15 }
  scaleDown:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300      # default 300 (wait 5 min)
    selectPolicy: Max
    policies:
    - { type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 15 }
```

### The task's manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: worker-hpa
  namespace: hpa-learn
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: worker
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 5
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 50
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
```

### How the stabilization window works
Over the last `stabilizationWindowSeconds`, the HPA keeps a history of computed desired-replica values.
- For **scaleDown**, it uses the **highest** recent recommendation as the floor → it won't scale in below a recent peak until that peak ages out of the window. This prevents a short lull from killing Pods you'll immediately need again.
- For **scaleUp**, the window default is `0` (scale out immediately on demand).

| Field | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` | 300 | wait up to 5 min of calm before scaling in |
| `scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds` | 0 | scale out without delay |
| `selectPolicy` | `Max` | which policy wins when several apply (`Disabled` freezes that direction) |

### Policies (rate limiting)
Each policy caps change per period:
| `type` | `value` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Pods` | N | change by at most N pods per `periodSeconds` |
| `Percent` | P | change by at most P% of current per `periodSeconds` |

`selectPolicy: Max` (default) picks the policy allowing the biggest change; `Min` the smallest; `Disabled` turns off scaling in that direction entirely.

### Inspecting
```bash
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa worker-hpa -o yaml | grep -A8 behavior
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa worker-hpa \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds}'; echo   # 300
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`behavior` is v2-only.** Add it under `spec`, a sibling of `metrics`.
- **Two independent directions** — `scaleUp` and `scaleDown`. Setting one does not change the other's defaults.
- **The window is smoothing, not a cooldown timer** — it uses the max recent recommendation; it does not simply "block for N seconds."
- **Defaults still apply** to anything you omit (scaleDown window defaults to 300 even if you don't set it — here you're making it explicit, which the grader checks).
- `selectPolicy: Disabled` on `scaleDown` means the HPA will **never** scale in — handy but easy to set by accident.
- Indentation: `scaleDown` is under `behavior`; `stabilizationWindowSeconds` is directly under `scaleDown`.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300   # wait 5 min of calm before scaling in
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: HPA shows <unknown>
questions.teach:
An HPA that reports `<unknown>` for CPU can't compute utilization because the target Deployment's container has **no CPU request** — utilization is a percentage *of the request*. Add a request so the HPA has a baseline.

**Gotcha:** HPA percentage metrics are relative to `requests`; without a request there's nothing to divide by.
questions.prompt:
HPA `broke-hpa` in `hpa-learn` targets Deployment `broke` but shows `<unknown>/50%` — it can't scale. Diagnose why and fix the **Deployment** so the HPA can compute CPU utilization. Don't delete the HPA.

Target: Deployment `broke`'s container has a CPU `requests` value set.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n hpa-learn describe hpa broke-hpa` → `<unknown>`. The `broke` Deployment has no CPU request. Add one: `kubectl -n hpa-learn set resources deployment/broke --requests=cpu=100m`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n hpa-learn set resources deployment/broke --requests=cpu=100m

questions.eli5:
Your thermostat is installed, but its screen just reads **`<unknown>`** where the temperature should be. It's not broken — it simply has **no reference point**. Imagine a thermostat that's supposed to say "you're at 80% of your target heat," but nobody ever told it what "100% heat" means. It can't turn a raw reading into a percentage, so it shrugs: `<unknown>`.

That's the HPA here. It shows `<unknown>/50%`. The HPA measures CPU as a **percentage of the CPU you requested** for the container. But the `broke` Deployment's container has **no CPU request at all** — so there's no "100%" to divide by, and the math is undefined.

The fix isn't on the HPA — it's on the **Deployment**. Give the container a CPU request so the HPA finally has a denominator:

```bash
kubectl -n hpa-learn set resources deployment/broke --requests=cpu=100m
```

Now `100m` is the baseline. If a Pod uses `50m`, that's 50% — and the HPA can finally compute and scale.

**Watch out for:**

- **The bug is on the Deployment, not the HPA.** Don't delete or recreate the HPA — add the request to the target workload.
- **`<unknown>` almost always means "missing request."** CPU utilization is a % of the request; no request → nothing to divide by.
- **`set resources` edits the Deployment template**, which triggers a rollout of fresh Pods that carry the request. Old Pods without it get replaced.
- **It must be the right resource** — a CPU-based HPA needs a **CPU** request; a memory HPA needs a memory request. Setting the wrong one won't fix it.
- On this bench there's **no metrics-server**, so even after the fix you may not see live numbers — the grade is that the request now exists.
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnose & fix: HPA shows `<unknown>` — full rundown

### Mental model
A Resource/`Utilization` HPA reports CPU as a **percentage of the container's CPU `request`**:
```
utilization% = actualCPU / requestedCPU × 100
```
If the container has **no CPU request**, the denominator is missing → the HPA cannot compute a percentage → `TARGETS` shows `<unknown>/50%` and it **refuses to scale**. The defect is on the **target Deployment**, not the HPA object.

### The symptom
```bash
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa broke-hpa
# NAME        REFERENCE          TARGETS         MINPODS  MAXPODS  REPLICAS
# broke-hpa   Deployment/broke   <unknown>/50%   1        5        1
kubectl -n hpa-learn describe hpa broke-hpa
# Conditions: ScalingActive False  FailedGetResourceMetric / missing request
```

### Diagnosis
```bash
kubectl -n hpa-learn get deploy broke \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'; echo
# {}      <-- no requests/limits -> no CPU request -> <unknown>
```

### The fix — add a CPU request to the Deployment
```bash
kubectl -n hpa-learn set resources deployment/broke --requests=cpu=100m
# verify:
kubectl -n hpa-learn get deploy broke \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests}'; echo
# {"cpu":"100m"}
```
`set resources` patches the pod **template**, so the Deployment rolls out new Pods that carry the request. Once a metrics source exists, the HPA computes utilization against `100m`.

### Why `<unknown>` happens — causes & fixes
| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| Container has **no request** for the metric | add `requests.cpu` / `requests.memory` |
| **metrics-server** not installed / not Ready | install metrics-server (cluster-level) |
| Wrong resource targeted (CPU HPA, only memory request set) | add the matching resource's request |
| Metric pipeline for custom/external down | fix the adapter |

On this bench there is **no metrics-server**, so values stay `<unknown>` regardless — the grading checks that the **request now exists**, which is the part a candidate controls.

### Alternative ways to add the request
```bash
# imperative (shown)
kubectl set resources deployment/broke --requests=cpu=100m -n hpa-learn

# edit
kubectl -n hpa-learn edit deployment broke     # add resources.requests.cpu: 100m

# patch
kubectl -n hpa-learn patch deployment broke --type=json -p \
 '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources","value":{"requests":{"cpu":"100m"}}}]'
```
YAML form on the container:
```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Fix the Deployment, not the HPA.** Do not delete/recreate the HPA — add the request to the workload.
- **`<unknown>` ≈ missing request** for Resource/Utilization metrics (or missing metrics-server). Check the request first.
- **Match the resource**: a CPU-% HPA needs a **CPU** request; adding only a memory request won't help.
- `requests` ≠ `limits`. Utilization is measured against **requests**; adding only a limit does not create a request (though a limit with no request often implies request=limit depending on setup — don't rely on it; set the request explicitly).
- `set resources` triggers a **rollout** — expect new Pods.
- Even after fixing, no metrics-server → still `<unknown>`; that's environmental, not your error.

### Quick reference
```bash
# diagnose
kubectl -n hpa-learn get hpa broke-hpa                                  # <unknown>/50%
kubectl -n hpa-learn get deploy broke -o jsonpath='{..resources}'       # {} -> no request

# fix
kubectl -n hpa-learn set resources deployment/broke --requests=cpu=100m
```
